Last week I did something simple. I set my phone's Google to Spanish, pretended I lived in Waterbury, and looked for a roofer.

I typed what a neighbor of mine would type: *techero en Waterbury CT*. Then *reparación de techos*. Then I opened Maps and scrolled.

I did the same in Danbury for a plumber, in Bridgeport for a mechanic, in Hartford and New Haven for an insurance agent and an HVAC company. Ten businesses, five cities, three searches each. I took screenshots of everything, because I wanted to be sure I wasn't imagining it.

## I wasn't.

## The good ones were the hardest to find

Here is what surprised me. The businesses missing from those searches were not bad businesses. Most of them were the opposite.

A family insurance agency with a perfect five-star rating sat somewhere around thirtieth on the map. A roofer with decades of work in the same city did not show up at all. A garage with more than a hundred reviews appeared only once, near the bottom of the list, under the wrong name.

None of them had done anything wrong. They had just never been told that a second line of customers was standing outside, looking for them in another language.

## What a Spanish search actually shows

When someone searches in Spanish, Google tries to match the words to something. A description. A list of services. A review. A page.

If your Google profile is empty, and many are, there is nothing to match. If your website is only in English, the same. So Google shows whoever gave it something to work with. Sometimes that is a smaller shop whose customers left reviews in Spanish. Sometimes it is a national company with a whole website in Spanish and a call center behind it.

And sometimes, and this one stayed with me, it is nobody. In one city I searched for an air conditioning technician in Spanish, and two of the three businesses Google offered fixed refrigerators, not heating systems. The space was empty. Whoever shows up first will have it.

## The numbers are not small

According to the Census, about 45% of people in Bridgeport and Hartford are Hispanic. In Waterbury it is close to 39%. In Danbury, about 32%.

Not all of them search in Spanish. Many are bilingual and search in English without thinking twice. But a lot of people, especially when the problem is urgent or expensive, a leaking roof, a car that won't start, an insurance claim, want to read about it in the language they think in. That is not a preference you can talk someone out of. It's just how people are.

## One review, answered in English

The detail I keep coming back to is small.

One of the businesses had exactly one review written in Spanish. A customer took the time to say something nice, in their own language. The owner answered, kindly, in English.

There's nothing wrong with that reply. But imagine being the next person reading it, deciding whether to call. You'd wonder if anyone on the other end would understand you. Most people don't call to find out.

## What fixing it looks like

It is less work than people think. In most cases it comes down to three things:

1. A page on your website in real Spanish, written for the searches people actually make, not run through a translator.
2. A Google profile that is complete, with a description and services, in English and in Spanish.
3. A clear way for a Spanish speaker to reach you. If someone on your team speaks Spanish, say so. If nobody does, a simple form and a few prepared replies are enough to keep that customer from going somewhere else.

That's it. No rebrand, no new website, no monthly bill unless you want one.
